stop.more: Stop is the only eight-sided sign, so you can recognise it even from behind or when it is dirty. It is used where a rolling 'slow down and look' is not enough — the view is blocked or cross traffic is fast.
where: Where a village road meets a busy highway
At a railway crossing approach or a blind junction in town

when.s: No other traffic is in sight
when.d: Still stop completely behind the line, look right, left and right again, then move off.

when.s: Your view is blocked by a wall or parked truck
when.d: Stop at the line first, then creep forward slowly until you can see, ready to stop again.

stop.mistake: Rolling slowly over the line without stopping — a 'rolling stop' is not a stop.

giveway.more: The point-down triangle means other traffic has priority over you. Unlike Stop, you need not stop if the way is clearly free — but you must be ready to.
where: Where a side road joins a main road
At the entry to a roundabout

when.s: A vehicle on the main road is close or you can't judge its speed
when.d: Stop behind the give-way line and wait for a bigger gap.

when.s: The main road is clear far in both directions
when.d: Enter at low speed without stopping, still watching both ways.

giveway.mistake: Pulling out and forcing a vehicle on the main road to brake.

noentry.more: A red disc with a white bar marks the 'wrong end' of a one-way road or an exit-only gate. Every vehicle coming the other way expects the road to be empty of oncoming traffic.
where: The exit end of a one-way street in town
The exit lane of a petrol pump, mall or toll plaza

when.s: Your map app tells you to go in
when.d: Trust the sign, not the app — take the next legal route.

when.s: You've already entered by mistake
when.d: Stop safely at the edge, switch on hazard lights and turn round only when it is safe; don't drive on against the traffic.

noentry.mistake: Entering 'just for a few metres' to reach a shop.

oneway.more: Placed at the start of a one-way road and repeated at junctions along it. Two-wheelers are not exempt.
where: Market roads and narrow streets in old town centres
Service roads beside flyovers

when.s: You missed your turn on a one-way road
when.d: Carry on with the flow and come back round the block.

when.s: You are crossing a one-way road on foot
when.d: Look mainly towards the traffic, but check the other way for wrong-way riders.

oneway.mistake: Riding a scooter a short distance against the arrow — oncoming drivers won't expect you.

allprohib.more: A plain red-ringed white circle closes the road to all vehicles in both directions, often temporarily for repairs, events or a pedestrian zone.
where: Pedestrian-only market streets
Roads closed for a festival, procession or repairs

when.s: You need to reach an address on that road
when.d: Park outside and walk in, or ask the officials on duty.

when.s: A local says it's fine to drive through
when.d: Follow the sign — it is there for people on foot or workers inside.

allprohib.mistake: Squeezing a two-wheeler past the board because 'it is only for cars'.

noahead.more: Usually placed where the road ahead becomes one-way against you, is closed, or crosses a busy carriageway that can't be crossed safely.
where: Junctions where the road ahead is one-way the other way
Median gaps on divided highways that allow turning only

when.s: Your destination is straight across
when.d: Turn left or right as allowed and use the next legal crossing or U-turn point.

when.s: Traffic police wave you straight on
when.d: A police officer's direction overrides the sign — go carefully as directed.

noahead.mistake: Darting straight across when the junction looks empty.

noright.more: Often at busy junctions where right-turning traffic would block the flow or cross fast oncoming lanes. It applies only at that junction.
where: Signal junctions on city arterial roads
Highway median openings near flyovers

when.s: You need to go right
when.d: Go straight, then turn at the next allowed point or use a loop of left turns.

when.s: You're in the right lane by mistake
when.d: Signal and move across early, or go straight; never turn from the wrong lane.

noright.mistake: Turning right anyway when no police are watching.

noleft.more: Used where a left turn would lead into a one-way road the wrong way, a closed road, or across a busy pedestrian area.
where: Junctions where the left road is one-way towards you
Gates of hospitals or schools that are entry-only from elsewhere

when.s: The left road leads to your destination
when.d: Continue and approach it from the side that allows entry.

when.s: A free-left lane is painted but this sign is up
when.d: The sign wins — don't turn left here.

nouturn.more: Turning round here would cut across fast traffic or block it. Look for the next median gap or roundabout.
where: Median gaps on busy highways
Near flyovers, bridges and blind bends

when.s: You've gone past your turning
when.d: Drive on to the next place where a U-turn is allowed or a roundabout.

when.s: The road looks empty
when.d: The ban still applies — fast traffic can appear in seconds.

nouturn.mistake: Making a U-turn in two or three movements across all lanes.

noovertake.more: Used where you can't see far enough ahead to pass safely: bends, crests, narrow bridges, ghat roads and school zones. It lasts until an 'end of overtaking prohibition' sign.
where: Ghat roads and hairpin sections
Approaches to narrow bridges and level crossings

when.s: A slow lorry is holding you up
when.d: Stay back with a good gap and wait for the end-of-restriction sign and a clear straight.

when.s: The vehicle ahead waves you past
when.d: Don't go — the sign applies to you whatever the other driver signals.

noovertake.mistake: Overtaking on a short straight inside the restricted stretch.

nohorn.more: Marks a silence zone around hospitals, schools, courts and some residential areas. Noise there disturbs patients, classes and proceedings.
where: Hospital and medical college roads
School and court premises

when.s: A pedestrian steps out in front of you
when.d: Brake — slowing down is the safe answer here, not the horn.

when.s: A real emergency needs a warning
when.d: A short warning to prevent a crash is reasonable; habitual honking is not.

nohorn.mistake: Honking at a slow vehicle or a red light inside the zone.

noparking.more: You may stop briefly to let someone in or out, but not leave the vehicle. It often applies only on the side of the road where the sign stands; a plate below may give times.
where: Near junctions, bus stops and hospital gates
Busy market roads where parked cars would block a lane

when.s: You need to pick someone up
when.d: Stop briefly with the engine running and stay with the vehicle; move off as soon as they're in.

when.s: The car park is full
when.d: Find another legal spot even if it's a walk away.

noparking.mistake: Leaving the car 'just for two minutes' to buy something.

nostop.more: Stricter than No parking: you may not stop even to drop someone off. It keeps traffic moving where a single stopped vehicle causes a jam or danger.
where: Flyovers, bridges and fast arterial roads
Approaches to junctions, toll plazas and airports

when.s: A passenger asks to get out here
when.d: Drive on to a place where stopping is allowed.

when.s: Your vehicle breaks down
when.d: Stopping is unavoidable — switch on hazard lights, get people to safety and set out a warning triangle if you have one.

nostop.mistake: Stopping on a flyover to make a phone call or check directions.

nopeds.more: Pedestrians are kept off roads where walking is dangerous, usually because a subway, foot-over bridge or another path is provided.
where: Expressways and access-controlled highways
Underpasses and flyovers with no footpath

when.s: You are walking and the bridge is far
when.d: Use it anyway — crossing a fast road on foot is one of the commonest ways people are killed.

when.s: You are driving and see someone walking there
when.d: Slow down and give them room; they may be lost or in trouble.

nopeds.mistake: Climbing over the median to save a walk to the foot-over bridge.

nocycles.more: Cycles are kept off roads where speed differences make cycling dangerous, typically fast highways and some flyovers.
where: Expressways and high-speed bypasses
Some flyovers and tunnels

when.s: You're cycling and the road is banned
when.d: Use the service road, a cycle track or another route.

when.s: You're driving and see a cyclist there anyway
when.d: Give them a wide berth and don't hoot to push them aside.

nocycles.mistake: Riding a cycle up a flyover because the service road is busy.

notruck.more: Keeps heavy goods vehicles out of town centres, narrow roads or weak bridges, sometimes only during certain hours shown on a plate.
where: City centre roads during the day
Narrow residential roads and old bridges

when.s: You drive a lorry and the plate shows hours
when.d: Wait until the allowed time or use the truck route.

when.s: You drive a car behind a lorry that ignored it
when.d: Keep extra distance; it may stop or reverse suddenly when stuck.

notruck.mistake: Taking a lorry through 'because the bypass is longer'.

nobullock.more: Slow animal-drawn carts are kept off busy or fast roads where they would hold up traffic and be at risk.
where: Town centres and highways
Bridges with heavy traffic

when.s: You drive a bullock cart
when.d: Use the village road or the service road beside the highway.

when.s: You meet a cart on the road anyway
when.d: Slow down, give it a wide berth and don't hoot — animals can bolt.

nobullock.mistake: Honking loudly to make the animal move faster.

nohandcart.more: Push and pull carts are kept off busy roads where they block a lane and are hard to see.
where: Main roads through markets
Flyovers and fast city roads

when.s: You push a handcart for a living
when.d: Use side lanes and the edge of quieter roads.

when.s: You're driving and a cart is ahead
when.d: Slow down and overtake only with plenty of room.

nohandcart.mistake: Pushing a heavily loaded cart up a flyover against fast traffic.

nomotor.more: Only non-motorised traffic — people on foot, cycles and carts — may use this road. Common in pedestrian zones, parks and heritage areas.
where: Park roads and beach promenades
Heritage streets and campus roads

when.s: You ride an electric scooter or e-bike with a motor
when.d: Treat it as a motor vehicle — keep out unless a sign says otherwise.

when.s: You need to deliver something inside
when.d: Park outside and carry it in, or ask for permission at the gate.

load.more: Protects bridges and weak roads. The number is the total weight of the vehicle plus everything in it, in tonnes.
where: Old bridges and culverts
Village roads with weak surfaces

when.s: Your lorry is fully loaded and may be over the limit
when.d: Don't risk it — take the alternative route even if it is longer.

when.s: You drive a car
when.d: The limit is far above a car's weight; it matters for lorries, buses and tractors with trailers.

load.mistake: Guessing the load instead of knowing it from the weighbridge or papers.

axle.more: Even if the total weight is within limits, too much weight on one axle can crack a bridge deck or road. Heavy loads must be spread evenly.
where: Bridges and flyovers
Roads with weak pavement

when.s: Your load is piled at the back
when.d: Redistribute it before the bridge so no single axle is overloaded.

when.s: You aren't sure of your axle loads
when.d: Check at a weighbridge that weighs axles, or take another route.

axle.mistake: Thinking that being under the total load limit is enough.

height.more: Warns of a low bridge, underpass, arch or overhead structure. The height includes anything on the roof — luggage, ladders, water tanks.
where: Railway under-bridges and old arches
Entrances of multi-storey car parks and petrol pump canopies

when.s: You have luggage on a roof carrier
when.d: Add its height to your vehicle's and compare before you go under.

when.s: You aren't sure you'll fit
when.d: Stop before the structure and check, or find another way — never 'try it slowly'.

height.mistake: Forgetting the extra height of a roof rack or a raised load.

width.more: Marks a narrow gap such as an old gateway, a narrow bridge or bollards. Mirrors and any load sticking out count.
where: Old town gates and narrow bridges
Bollards at the entry of lanes

when.s: You drive a wide vehicle or carry a wide load
when.d: Measure it and use another route if in doubt.

when.s: Your car just fits
when.d: Fold the mirrors if needed and go through slowly and straight.

width.mistake: Ignoring a load that sticks out to the sides.

length.more: Used where long vehicles can't make a tight turn or bend, such as hill roads and narrow junctions.
where: Ghat roads with tight hairpins
Narrow junctions in old towns

when.s: You drive a long bus or a truck with a trailer
when.d: Use the route marked for long vehicles.

when.s: A long vehicle is stuck at a bend ahead
when.d: Stay well back and give it room to reverse.

length.mistake: Trying to make it round 'with a few shunts' and blocking the road.

speed.more: The number is a maximum, not a target. It applies from the sign until another speed sign or an end-of-limit sign. Lower limits are common near schools, towns and bends.
where: Entering a town or village on a highway
Near schools, hospitals and ghat sections

when.s: It's raining or foggy
when.d: Drive well below the limit — the number is for good conditions.

when.s: Traffic around you is going faster
when.d: Stay at or below the limit; keep left and let others pass.

speed.mistake: Braking hard at a speed camera and speeding up again straight after.

endrestr.more: The grey or black diagonal stripes cancel the restriction shown before — such as a speed limit or no overtaking. General rules still apply.
where: After a school zone or road works
At the end of a ghat section or town limits

when.s: A no-overtaking stretch ends
when.d: You may overtake again, but only when you can see the road is clear for long enough.

when.s: A low speed limit ends
when.d: Build up speed gradually to suit the road — not to the maximum straight away.

endrestr.mistake: Treating it as 'no limits at all'.

cahead.more: Blue circles give orders. This one forbids turning at the next junction — usually because the side roads are one-way or turning would block traffic.
where: Approach lanes at signal junctions
Flyover ramps and underpass entries

when.s: You wanted to turn
when.d: Go straight and turn at the next place that allows it.

when.s: You're in a lane marked for turning but the sign shows straight only
when.d: The sign applies to the whole road at that point; go straight.

cahead.mistake: Cutting across at the last moment to make a turn.

cleft.more: Every vehicle at this point must turn left — straight on and right are not allowed, often because the road ahead is one-way against you.
where: One-way systems in town centres
Slip roads that lead off a junction

when.s: Your destination is straight ahead
when.d: Turn left as ordered, then find a route back.

when.s: Pedestrians are crossing the road you're turning into
when.d: Wait for them — turning traffic gives way to people crossing.

cleft.mistake: Going straight on because 'the road ahead looks open'.

cright.more: Every vehicle must turn right here. Right turns cross oncoming traffic, so they need the most care.
where: One-way grids in cities
Junctions where the road ahead is closed

when.s: Oncoming traffic is heavy
when.d: Wait in position, wheels straight, until there's a safe gap.

when.s: A motorcycle could be hidden behind an oncoming bus
when.d: Look past it before you commit to the turn.

cright.mistake: Waiting with the wheels already turned — a shunt from behind pushes you into oncoming traffic.

caheadleft.more: Two permitted directions; turning right is banned. Pick your lane early so you aren't forced to cut across.
where: Busy signal junctions where right turns are diverted
Exits of flyovers

when.s: You need to go right
when.d: Go straight or left and use the next legal turn.

when.s: You're in the left lane and want to go straight
when.d: Check the lane arrows — some left lanes are turn-only.

caheadleft.mistake: Turning right from the straight lane.

caheadright.more: Straight on or right only; left is banned — perhaps the left road is one-way towards you.
where: Junctions with a one-way road on the left
Service road entries

when.s: You need to go left
when.d: Continue and come round another way.

when.s: You're turning right across traffic
when.d: Give way to oncoming vehicles and people crossing.

caheadright.mistake: Using the left turn because 'it's quicker'.

ckeepleft.more: Placed on traffic islands, median ends and around obstructions. Passing on the wrong side puts you head-on with oncoming traffic.
where: Ends of medians and traffic islands
Around road works or a broken-down vehicle

when.s: The left side looks narrow
when.d: Slow down and pass on the left anyway; never use the right side.

when.s: A pedestrian is waiting on the island
when.d: Expect them to step off; slow down as you pass.

ckeepleft.mistake: Going round the 'short way' on the right of an island.

ckeepright.more: Less common: used where the only safe passage is on the right of an obstruction, for example at work zones or on one-way roads.
where: Road works blocking the left of a lane
One-way roads with an island on the left

when.s: Oncoming traffic could be on the right
when.d: Check carefully — on a two-way road give way before moving out.

when.s: Workers are on the left
when.d: Pass slowly with a wide gap.

ckeepright.mistake: Squeezing through on the left because it seems shorter.

chorn.more: Tells you to give a short horn warning where others can't see you coming — blind bends and crests on hill roads.
where: Blind hairpins on ghat roads
Narrow hill roads with walls or rock on the inside

when.s: You approach the blind bend
when.d: Give one short honk, slow down and keep left.

when.s: You hear a horn from round the bend
when.d: Slow down and keep well left; a vehicle is coming.

chorn.mistake: Long, continuous honking while speeding into the bend.

ccycle.more: A track reserved for cycles. Motor vehicles must keep out and must not park on it.
where: Beside new city roads and lake promenades
Campus roads and smart-city corridors

when.s: You're turning across the cycle track
when.d: Look for cyclists coming from behind on your side before you turn.

when.s: A two-wheeler is riding on the track
when.d: Don't follow it — it's only for cycles.

ccycle.mistake: Parking a car or scooter on the cycle track 'for a minute'.

hairR.more: A hairpin bends back on itself to the right, common on ghat roads. Large vehicles need the whole width of the road to get round, and you can't see what's coming.
where: Ghat roads to hill stations such as Munnar or Wayanad
Mountain passes with numbered hairpins

when.s: A bus or lorry is coming round the hairpin towards you
when.d: Stop on your side in good time and let it complete the turn, even if it uses your lane.

when.s: You are going downhill
when.d: Change to a low gear before the bend and brake gently on the straight, not in the turn.

hairR.mistake: Cutting the inside of the hairpin to save time — that's where oncoming vehicles swing.

hairL.more: A hairpin bends back on itself to the left, common on ghat roads. Large vehicles need the whole width of the road to get round, and you can't see what's coming.
where: Ghat roads to hill stations such as Munnar or Wayanad
Mountain passes with numbered hairpins

when.s: A bus or lorry is coming round the hairpin towards you
when.d: Stop on your side in good time and let it complete the turn, even if it uses your lane.

when.s: You are going downhill
when.d: Change to a low gear before the bend and brake gently on the straight, not in the turn.

hairL.mistake: Cutting the inside of the hairpin to save time — that's where oncoming vehicles swing.

curveR.more: A gentle curve to the right. Gentle doesn't mean you can keep any speed — at night or in rain, grip and sight are reduced.
where: Highways through plantations and paddy fields
Rural roads following a river or hill

when.s: You're approaching faster than feels comfortable
when.d: Brake on the straight before the curve, then hold a steady speed through it.

when.s: A vehicle ahead is slow on the curve
when.d: Don't overtake until you can see the road beyond is clear.

curveR.mistake: Braking hard in the middle of the curve.

curveL.more: A gentle curve to the left. Gentle doesn't mean you can keep any speed — at night or in rain, grip and sight are reduced.
where: Highways through plantations and paddy fields
Rural roads following a river or hill

when.s: You're approaching faster than feels comfortable
when.d: Brake on the straight before the curve, then hold a steady speed through it.

when.s: A vehicle ahead is slow on the curve
when.d: Don't overtake until you can see the road beyond is clear.

curveL.mistake: Braking hard in the middle of the curve.

bendR.more: A sharp, near right-angle turn to the right ahead. The road may look like it carries straight on, especially at night.
where: Village roads turning round a field or a temple wall
Highways with a sudden turn at a bridge

when.s: It's dark and the road edge is hard to see
when.d: Slow right down; follow the chevrons and reflectors round the turn.

when.s: A side road joins at the bend
when.d: Expect vehicles to come out; be ready to stop.

bendR.mistake: Arriving too fast and running wide into the oncoming lane.

bendL.more: A sharp, near right-angle turn to the left ahead. The road may look like it carries straight on, especially at night.
where: Village roads turning round a field or a temple wall
Highways with a sudden turn at a bridge

when.s: It's dark and the road edge is hard to see
when.d: Slow right down; follow the chevrons and reflectors round the turn.

when.s: A side road joins at the bend
when.d: Expect vehicles to come out; be ready to stop.

bendL.mistake: Arriving too fast and running wide into the oncoming lane.

revR.more: Two bends close together: first right, then the other way. Speed that suits the first bend may be too much for the second.
where: Hill roads and river crossings
Roads around old buildings in towns

when.s: You can't see past the second bend
when.d: Keep to your lane and slow enough to stop within what you can see.

when.s: You're riding a two-wheeler
when.d: Brake upright before the first bend; don't brake while leaned over between them.

revL.more: Two bends close together: first left, then the other way. Speed that suits the first bend may be too much for the second.
where: Hill roads and river crossings
Roads around old buildings in towns

when.s: You can't see past the second bend
when.d: Keep to your lane and slow enough to stop within what you can see.

when.s: You're riding a two-wheeler
when.d: Brake upright before the first bend; don't brake while leaned over between them.

ascent.more: A steep climb ahead. Heavy vehicles slow down a lot, and you may have to stop and restart on the slope.
where: Ghat roads and approaches to hill towns
Ramps of flyovers and river bridges

when.s: A loaded lorry ahead is crawling
when.d: Keep a bigger gap — it may stop or roll back slightly when changing gear.

when.s: You must stop on the slope
when.d: Use the handbrake for the restart so you don't roll back.

ascent.mistake: Staying in a high gear until the engine struggles, then changing down in a panic.

descent.more: A steep downhill. Gravity keeps speeding you up, and long braking can overheat the brakes until they fade.
where: Ghat roads coming down from the hills
Long bridge approaches

when.s: Your speed keeps creeping up
when.d: Shift to a lower gear and use short, firm brake applications instead of riding the brake.

when.s: The brakes feel soft or smell hot
when.d: Stop in a safe place and let them cool before going on.

narrow.more: The carriageway gets narrower — two lanes may become one, or the shoulders disappear.
where: Where a widened highway meets an old section
Village roads between buildings

when.s: A wide vehicle is coming the other way
when.d: Slow down and pull to the left early; stop if needed and let it pass.

when.s: You're side by side with another vehicle
when.d: Ease off and let it merge ahead rather than racing for the gap.

narrow.mistake: Speeding up to get through before the oncoming vehicle.

widen.more: The road becomes wider — often from two lanes to four. Vehicles behind may start overtaking and others may change lanes.
where: Start of a four-lane section on a highway
Approaches to a town bypass

when.s: Faster vehicles want to pass
when.d: Keep left and hold a steady line.

when.s: Lanes aren't marked yet
when.d: Stay predictable; don't drift into the middle.

widen.mistake: Swinging out to overtake before the extra lane has actually started.

bridge.more: The bridge is narrower than the road leading to it, so vehicles must squeeze in, and there's no shoulder to escape to.
where: Old bridges over rivers and canals
Culverts on village roads

when.s: A bus is already on the bridge coming towards you
when.d: Wait before the bridge until it's off.

when.s: You're both arriving at the same time
when.d: Slow down; the vehicle nearer the bridge or with the clearer path usually goes first — don't race.

bridge.mistake: Overtaking on the approach to the bridge.

sideR.more: A minor road joins from the right. You have priority, but drivers coming out may not see you or may misjudge your speed.
where: Village roads joining a state highway
Lanes coming out between shops and houses

when.s: A vehicle is waiting at the side road
when.d: Ease off and cover the brake; be ready if it pulls out.

when.s: You want to overtake near the junction
when.d: Don't — a vehicle may turn out or in just as you're alongside.

sideR.mistake: Holding full speed because you 'have priority'.

sideL.more: A minor road joins from the left. You have priority, but drivers coming out may not see you or may misjudge your speed.
where: Village roads joining a state highway
Lanes coming out between shops and houses

when.s: A vehicle is waiting at the side road
when.d: Ease off and cover the brake; be ready if it pulls out.

when.s: You want to overtake near the junction
when.d: Don't — a vehicle may turn out or in just as you're alongside.

sideL.mistake: Holding full speed because you 'have priority'.

tj.more: Your road ends ahead and you must turn left or right. At night the end of the road can come up suddenly.
where: Where a village road ends at a highway
Ends of roads in towns and beside rivers

when.s: You don't know which way to turn
when.d: Slow down early and read the direction board before the junction.

when.s: Traffic on the road ahead has priority
when.d: Stop if needed and wait for a safe gap.

tj.mistake: Arriving fast at night and overshooting into the road ahead.

yj.more: The road splits in two. The fork can be hard to read at speed, and drivers who chose late swerve across.
where: Highway forks towards two towns
Splits at the foot of a flyover

when.s: You aren't sure which branch to take
when.d: Choose early from the signboards; if you miss it, carry on and turn round safely later.

when.s: A vehicle ahead hesitates at the fork
when.d: Hold back; it may cut across in front of you.

yj.mistake: Changing your mind at the nose of the fork.

stag.more: Two side roads join a short distance apart on opposite sides, so vehicles may cross your road in two steps.
where: Market towns on state highways
Residential areas with offset lanes

when.s: A vehicle comes out of the first side road
when.d: Expect it to cross straight over into the second; slow down.

when.s: You're turning between the two roads
when.d: Signal clearly and check both ways twice.

stag.mistake: Watching only one side and missing the vehicle from the other.

crossRd.more: A four-way junction without signals. Many crashes happen here because each driver assumes the other will stop.
where: Rural junctions on state highways
Grid roads in towns

when.s: You think you have priority
when.d: Slow down anyway and look both ways — the other driver may not agree.

when.s: Hedges or buildings hide the side roads
when.d: Approach slowly enough to stop.

crossRd.mistake: Crossing at full speed because the road you're on looks bigger.

round.more: Traffic goes round clockwise (to the left) and vehicles already on the roundabout have priority over those entering.
where: Town centres and major junctions
Bypass interchanges

when.s: You're going right (the third exit)
when.d: Approach in the right lane, keep to the inside, and move out after the exit before yours, signalling left.

when.s: A bus is going round beside you
when.d: Don't ride alongside it — let it exit first.

round.mistake: Entering without looking right, or stopping on the roundabout to read signs.

major.more: Your road meets a bigger, busier road that has priority. Expect fast traffic from both sides.
where: Village roads meeting a national highway
Service roads joining a main road

when.s: Traffic on the major road is fast and continuous
when.d: Wait patiently for a safe gap; don't edge out into it.

when.s: You need to cross the major road
when.d: Make sure both directions are clear, or turn and use a proper crossing point.

major.mistake: Pulling out because 'they'll slow down for me'.

dip.more: A sudden dip, often where a stream crosses the road. A car in the dip is hidden from view, and the bump at the bottom can unsettle the vehicle.
where: Causeways across streams on rural roads
Undulating plantation roads

when.s: You can't see the bottom of the dip
when.d: Slow down and keep left — an oncoming vehicle may be hidden there.

when.s: Water is lying in the dip
when.d: Check the depth before you go in; don't go into flowing water.

hump.more: A speed breaker or raised hump ahead. Many aren't painted, so this sign may be your only warning.
where: Outside schools, hospitals and junctions in villages
Entries to housing colonies and campuses

when.s: You're on a two-wheeler with a pillion
when.d: Slow right down and cross it straight, standing slightly on the footrests if needed.

when.s: The vehicle ahead brakes suddenly for the hump
when.d: Keep enough gap that you don't have to brake hard too.

hump.mistake: Swerving to the edge of the road to dodge the hump.

slip.more: The surface may lose grip, especially in the first rain after a dry spell when oil and dust float up, or where mud or leaves lie.
where: Hill roads in the monsoon
Approaches to fuel stations and markets

when.s: It has just started raining
when.d: Double your following gap and brake, accelerate and steer gently.

when.s: The car starts to slide
when.d: Ease off the accelerator, look where you want to go and steer smoothly; don't slam the brakes.

slip.mistake: Braking hard and turning at the same time.

gravel.more: Loose chips on the surface reduce grip and get flung up by tyres, cracking windscreens and hurting riders.
where: Freshly resurfaced roads
Quarry and construction areas

when.s: You're following another vehicle
when.d: Drop well back so stones from its tyres don't hit you.

when.s: You're riding a two-wheeler
when.d: Slow down before bends and avoid sudden braking; the front tyre can wash out.

gravel.mistake: Overtaking and spraying stones at the vehicle you pass.

rocks.more: Rocks can fall from a cutting or slope, especially during and after heavy rain. They may already be lying on the road.
where: Ghat roads through cuttings
Hill highways in the monsoon

when.s: You see small stones trickling down
when.d: Don't stop below the slope; drive on carefully and report it if it's serious.

when.s: A rock is lying in your lane round a bend
when.d: Slow enough on these stretches to stop or steer round safely.

rocks.mistake: Stopping under the cliff to take photographs.

cattle.more: Cows, buffaloes or goats are often on or beside the road, especially near villages, at dusk and on market days. Animals move unpredictably.
where: Village roads and highways through farmland
Near dairy farms and cattle markets

when.s: Animals are standing in the road
when.d: Slow to walking pace and pass with a wide gap; wait if they block the road.

when.s: It's dusk or dark
when.d: Slow down — dark animals are very hard to see and their eyes may not reflect.

cattle.mistake: Honking loudly — startled animals may run into your path.

pedx.more: Warns of a zebra crossing ahead that you may not see yet — over a crest, round a bend or in busy streets.
where: Town roads near bus stops and markets
Highways passing through villages

when.s: People are waiting at the kerb
when.d: Slow down and stop to let them cross; don't wave them out into another lane's traffic.

when.s: A vehicle has stopped at the crossing in the next lane
when.d: Assume someone is crossing in front of it — stop too.

pedx.mistake: Overtaking a vehicle that has stopped at a crossing.

school.more: A school is close by. Children are small, hard to see between parked vehicles and may run out without looking — especially at start and end of school.
where: Roads outside schools in towns and villages
Near school bus stops on highways

when.s: It's school opening or closing time
when.d: Drive at a crawl and be ready to stop; watch for children between vehicles.

when.s: A school bus has stopped
when.d: Pass very slowly or wait — children may cross in front of it.

school.mistake: Keeping normal speed because school seems over for the day.

work.more: Road works ahead: workers, machines, loose material and narrowed lanes. Workers often have their backs to traffic.
where: Highway widening projects
Pipe-laying and resurfacing in towns

when.s: A flagman shows STOP
when.d: Stop and wait until you are waved on.

when.s: The lane is coned off
when.d: Merge early and in turn, and pass the workers slowly.

work.mistake: Speeding through the work zone once you're past the flagman.

ferry.more: The road leads to a ferry or jankar — common on Kerala's backwaters. There may be a queue, a ramp and a drop into water.
where: Backwater crossings such as those in Alappuzha and Kochi
River crossings without a bridge

when.s: You're driving onto the ferry
when.d: Follow the ferry staff's signals exactly, go slowly, then apply the handbrake and switch off.

when.s: There's a queue
when.d: Wait in line with a gap; don't overtake towards the ramp.

ferry.mistake: Driving down the ramp before the ferry is tied up.

cyclex.more: A cycle track or route crosses the road. Cyclists may come out at speed, especially schoolchildren.
where: Where a cycle track crosses a road in new towns
Near schools and colleges

when.s: Cyclists are approaching the crossing
when.d: Slow down and let them cross.

when.s: You're turning across a cycle route
when.d: Check for cyclists coming from behind on your left.

cyclex.mistake: Assuming cyclists will always stop for cars.

gap.more: An opening in the median where vehicles cross or U-turn. Turning vehicles may move slowly across your lanes.
where: Divided highways through towns
Opposite petrol pumps and side roads

when.s: A vehicle is waiting in the gap
when.d: Ease off and move away from the median lane if you can — it may pull out.

when.s: You want to use the gap
when.d: Signal early, slow down in the right lane and give way to oncoming traffic before crossing.

gap.mistake: Driving fast in the lane next to the median past an occupied gap.

x2_notonga.more: Horse-drawn vehicles are kept off this road, usually because they are slow and horses can be startled by fast traffic. Other traffic is unaffected.
where: Highways and busy city roads
Flyovers

when.s: You are driving one of these: horse-drawn vehicles
when.d: Turn off before the sign and use the alternative route or service road.

when.s: You see one on the road anyway
when.d: Give it room and patience — it may be looking for a way off.

x2_notractor.more: Tractors are kept off this road, usually because they are slow, wide and may carry trailers that block lanes. Other traffic is unaffected.
where: Expressways and city centres
Bridges with weight limits

when.s: You are driving one of these: tractors
when.d: Turn off before the sign and use the alternative route or service road.

when.s: You see one on the road anyway
when.d: Give it room and patience — it may be looking for a way off.

x2_nomoto.more: Scooters and motorcycles are kept off this road, usually because the road is fast, access-controlled, or a flyover where riders are at high risk. Other traffic is unaffected.
where: Some expressways and elevated roads
Certain flyovers and tunnels

when.s: You are driving one of these: scooters and motorcycles
when.d: Turn off before the sign and use the alternative route or service road.

when.s: You see one on the road anyway
when.d: Give it room and patience — it may be looking for a way off.

x2_nobus.more: Buses are kept off this road, usually because the road is too narrow, has low structures, or buses have their own route. Other traffic is unaffected.
where: Narrow residential roads
Old town lanes and low underpasses

when.s: You are driving one of these: buses
when.d: Turn off before the sign and use the alternative route or service road.

when.s: You see one on the road anyway
when.d: Give it room and patience — it may be looking for a way off.

x2_noauto.more: Auto-rickshaws are kept off this road, usually because the road is fast or access-controlled, or autos would stop and block traffic. Other traffic is unaffected.
where: Expressways and some flyovers
Airport and station approach roads

when.s: You are driving one of these: auto-rickshaws
when.d: Turn off before the sign and use the alternative route or service road.

when.s: You see one on the road anyway
when.d: Give it room and patience — it may be looking for a way off.

x2_nocycrick.more: Cycle-rickshaws are kept off this road, usually because they are slow and unprotected on a fast road. Other traffic is unaffected.
where: Main arterial roads
Flyovers and bridges

when.s: You are driving one of these: cycle-rickshaws
when.d: Turn off before the sign and use the alternative route or service road.

when.s: You see one on the road anyway
when.d: Give it room and patience — it may be looking for a way off.

x2_minspeed.more: A blue circle with a number sets a minimum, used on fast roads where very slow vehicles would cause dangerous braking and lane changes behind them.
where: Expressways and access-controlled highways
Fast lanes of some elevated roads

when.s: Your vehicle can't keep up, or a load makes you slow
when.d: Use another road, or the leftmost lane where one exists.

when.s: Traffic is jammed
when.d: You can drive slower than the minimum — it never forces you to be unsafe.

x2_minspeed.mistake: Crawling in the right lane on an expressway.

x2_endspeed.more: Ends the specific limit that was posted before. The general limits for that type of road and vehicle still apply.
where: Leaving a town or a school zone
After road works or a ghat section

when.s: You've left a 30 km/h school zone
when.d: Speed up gradually to a speed that suits the road and traffic.

when.s: Weather is poor
when.d: Stay slow — ending a limit doesn't make the road safer.

x2_endspeed.mistake: Accelerating hard the moment you pass the sign.

x2_endovertake.more: Marks where a no-overtaking stretch ends. Overtaking becomes allowed — not automatically safe.
where: After a ghat section or a series of bends
Past a narrow bridge or a school zone

when.s: You've been behind a slow lorry for kilometres
when.d: Wait for a long, clear straight with no junctions, then overtake decisively.

when.s: Oncoming traffic is close
when.d: Stay behind; the sign only removes the ban.

x2_endovertake.mistake: Pulling out the instant you see the sign without checking ahead.

x2_giveoncoming.more: On a single-lane stretch — narrow bridge, culvert or road works — traffic from the other side goes first. The opposite end usually has a 'priority over oncoming' sign.
where: Narrow bridges on village roads
Single-lane stretches through road works

when.s: An oncoming vehicle has entered the narrow part
when.d: Stop in the wider area before it and wait.

when.s: The narrow part is empty and you can see the far end
when.d: Go through steadily without stopping in the middle.

x2_giveoncoming.mistake: Racing an oncoming vehicle to the narrow section.

x2_passeither.more: Both sides of the island or obstruction are open in your direction — common on one-way roads and divided carriageways.
where: Islands on one-way roads
Toll plaza approaches and bridge piers

when.s: Vehicles are passing on both sides
when.d: Choose a side early and hold your line; don't switch at the last moment.

when.s: A two-wheeler is filtering on one side
when.d: Pass on the other side with room.

x2_passeither.mistake: Swerving from one side to the other just before the island.
